title: Bar (establishment)
description: Establishment serving alcoholic beverages for consumption on the premises
wiki_lead:
A bar, also known as a saloon, a tavern or tippling house, or sometimes as a pub (public house) or club, is a retail business that serves alcoholic beverages, such as beer, wine, liquor, cocktails, and other beverages such as mineral water and soft drinks. Bars often also sell snacks, such as chips (crisps) or peanuts, for consumption on their premises. Some types of bars, such as pubs, may also serve food from a restaurant menu.
The term "bar" derives from a metal or wooden bar (barrier) often located along the length of a countertop where drinks are prepared and served by a bartender from an available selection of liquors behind them; these countertops are built with a depth between 18–24 inches (0.46–0.61 m)), smaller than that of an ordinary dining table. The term bar eventually extended to the entirety of the establishment in which the bar counter was located.
wiki_excerpt:
A bar, also known as a saloon, a tavern or tippling house, or sometimes as a pub (public house) or club, is a retail business that serves alcoholic beverages, such as beer, wine, liquor, cocktails, and other beverages such as mineral water and soft drinks. Bars often also sell snacks, such as chips (crisps) or peanuts, for consumption on their premises. Some types of bars, such as pubs, may also serve food from a restaurant menu.
The term "bar" derives from a metal or wooden bar (barrier) often located along the length of a countertop where drinks are prepared and served by a bartender from an available selection of liquors behind them; these countertops are built with a depth between 18–24 inches (0.46–0.61 m)), smaller than that of an ordinary dining table. The term bar eventually extended to the entirety of the establishment in which the bar counter was located.


History

There have been many different names for public drinking spaces throughout history. In the Thirteen Colonies of North America, a tavern was a meeting place. During the 19th century, saloons were very important to the leisure time of the working class. Today, even when an establishment uses a different name, such as "tavern" or "saloon" or, in the United Kingdom, a "pub", the area of the establishment where the bartender pours or mixes beverages is normally called "the bar".
The sale and/or consumption of alcoholic beverages was prohibited in the first half of the 20th century in several countries. In the United States, illegal bars during Prohibition were called "speakeasies", "blind pigs", and "blind tigers".


Legal restrictions
Laws in many U.S. states, such as California, prohibit minors from entering a bar. In the UK, minors are permitted to be in a bar, though there are many bars that also serve food. In many jurisdictions, if those under legal drinking age are allowed to enter, as is the case with pubs that serve food, they are not allowed to drink; in the U.S., there are 8 states where children may drink in a pub if accompanied by their parents. In some jurisdictions, bars cannot serve a patron who is already intoxicated. Cities and towns usually have legal restrictions on where bars may be located and on the types of alcohol they may serve to their customers. Some bars may have a license to serve beer and wine, but not hard liquor. In some jurisdictions, patrons buying alcohol must also order food. In some jurisdictions, bar owners have a legal liability for the conduct of patrons who they serve (this liability may arise in cases of driving under the influence which cause injuries or deaths).
Many Islamic countries prohibit bars as well as the possession or sale of alcohol for religious reasons, while others, including Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, allow bars in some specific areas, but only permit non-Muslims to drink in them.


Types

A bar's owners and managers choose the bar's name, décor, drink menu, lighting, and other elements which they think will attract a certain kind of patron. However, they have only limited influence over who patronizes their establishment. Thus, a bar originally intended for one demographic profile can become popular with another. For example, a gay or lesbian bars with a dance or disco floor might, over time, attract an increasingly heterosexual clientele, or a blues bar may become a biker bar if most its patrons are bikers. Bars can also be an integral part of larger venues. For example, hotels, casinos and nightclubs are usually home to one or several bars. Other types of bar include:

A cocktail lounge is an upscale bar that is typically located within a hotel, restaurant or airport.
A full bar serves liquor, cocktails, wine, and beer.
A wine bar is a bar that focuses on wine rather than on beer or liquor. Patrons of these bars may taste wines before deciding to buy them. Some wine bars also serve small plates of food or other snacks.
A beer bar focuses on beer, particularly craft beer, rather than on wine
grok_lead: A bar is a licensed retail establishment primarily engaged in selling alcoholic beverages for on-premises consumption, typically featuring a counter where patrons are served by a bartender. These venues often provide limited food options, such as snacks or simple meals, to complement drinks and comply with local licensing requirements. Distinguished by their focus on alcohol salesâfrequently deriving 75% or more of revenue from beveragesâbars serve as social gathering spots for conversation, entertainment, and relaxation. The concept of bars traces its roots to ancient civilizations where communal drinking houses facilitated social and commercial exchange, evolving into structured establishments by the 17th century in Europe and colonial America, where wooden or metal counters acted as barriers between servers and customers to maintain order. In the United States, bars emerged from taverns that offered lodging and meals alongside alcohol, adapting post-Prohibition (1920â1933) into modern forms emphasizing rapid service and ambiance. Globally, variations like British pubs prioritize community ties and fuller menus, while American bars often cater to quicker, drink-focused visits, reflecting regional cultural norms and regulatory frameworks. Bars operate under stringent government regulations, including age restrictions, operating hours, and capacity limits, aimed at mitigating alcohol-related harms such as violence and public disorder, with empirical studies showing that restrictions like later closing times correlate with increased assault densities near venues. Despite these risksâevidenced by higher incidences of aggression in bar settingsâbars contribute economically through employment and tourism, and socially by fostering interpersonal connections, though data underscores the need for evidence-based oversight rather than blanket moralizing.
